source: 경희대 편입영어 2021~2026학년도 기출 출제 유형(문항 수·영역·문제 꼴, VocabFactory 분석)을 분석해 dailyfreetoolbox 가 새로 만든 연습 문제

passages.text:
For centuries, the fishing town of Grindavik on Iceland's Reykjanes Peninsula lived placidly beside a volcanic system that had been dormant for approximately eight hundred years. That changed abruptly. In November 2023, after hundreds of tremors opened deep fissures in its streets, the town's nearly four thousand residents were compelled to leave. Since then, the peninsula has erupted again and again, with fountains of lava gushing from fissures that open with scant warning.
Iceland has responded with an unusual amalgam of science and engineering. Seismologists and geologists track the bulging of the ground as magma accumulates beneath it, which allows the authorities to predict many eruptions days in advance. Meanwhile, construction crews have erected long earthen embankments around the town and a nearby geothermal power plant in the hope of deflecting the lava. The walls have diverted several flows, although in January 2024 lava crossed into the edge of the town and razed a few houses.
Most residents have not returned. Geologists warn that the peninsula may have entered an active period that could last for decades or even centuries, as comparable periods did in the distant past. For the town, the question is no longer whether the volcano will erupt but whether people can ____.

In July 1518, a woman named Frau Troffea stepped into a street in Strasbourg and began to dance. She did not stop for days. Within weeks, according to chronicles of the time, dozens and perhaps hundreds of townspeople had joined her, dancing until they succumbed to exhaustion. Some chronicles assert that people died, though historians treat these reports with circumspection.
The city's authorities responded in a way that seems astounding today. Believing that the dancers would recuperate only if they danced the affliction out of their bodies, officials commandeered guildhalls, hired musicians, and even built a wooden stage. The measure <u>backfired</u>: the music and spectacle appear to have drawn still more people into the frenzy. Eventually the council reversed course, prohibited public music, and sent the afflicted to a shrine of Saint Vitus in the hills.
What provoked the outbreak remains disputed. One theory implicates ergot, a fungus on damp rye that can induce hallucinations and spasms, but critics note that ergot poisoning rarely allows sustained, coordinated movement. The historian John Waller has contended instead that the dancing was a form of mass psychogenic illness, precipitated by years of famine and disease in a populace that believed a wrathful saint could curse sinners with uncontrollable dancing.

Machine translation has improved so markedly in recent years that a traveler can now sustain a halting conversation with a shopkeeper through a phone app, each speaking into the device in turn. For mundane tasks such as reading a menu, a product manual, or a casual email, many people no longer see any need for a human translator. Translation agencies have felt the change. A growing share of their work now consists of post-editing, in which a professional rectifies text that a machine has already produced, usually for (A) ____ pay than a translation done from scratch.
Interpreters, who convey spoken language in real time, contend that their work is harder to automate than it appears. In a courtroom, a hospital, or a fraught diplomatic meeting, a single mistranslated word can alter a verdict, a diagnosis, or the course of a negotiation. Interpreters also do more than swap words. They notice when a witness is bewildered, when a patient is too abashed to articulate a symptom, or when a polite phrase in one language would sound like an insult in another.
For this reason, several professional associations insist that machines should remain (B) ____ in such high-stakes settings, assisting human interpreters rather than replacing them. Whether that boundary will endure as the software keeps improving is far from certain.

Many pedestrians press the button at a crosswalk and then press it again, as if repetition might expedite the signal. In a large number of cities, the effort is squandered. When traffic signals became computerized and synchronized to the flow of cars, engineers in places such as New York disconnected many crosswalk buttons or set them to work only at night, but they rarely bothered to remove the buttons themselves. A 2004 newspaper inquiry estimated that most of the crosswalk buttons in New York City no longer did anything at all.
Comparable devices appear elsewhere. Some office thermostats are locked at a fixed temperature, and the door-close buttons in many elevators have little or no effect during normal operation. Psychologists posit that such buttons may nonetheless serve a purpose. Since the work of Ellen Langer in the 1970s, researchers have documented an illusion of control: people feel calmer and more patient when they believe their actions sway an outcome, even when they do not. A button that does nothing may still ____ the frustration of waiting.
Critics reply that the practice is quietly deceptive and that public money would be better spent on countdown timers, which tell pedestrians plainly how long they must wait.

In the spring of 2024, parts of the American Midwest witnessed a rare natural event. Two broods of periodical cicadas, one that emerges every 13 years and another that appears every 17 years, came out of the ground in the same season, the first such joint emergence since 1803. (A) In a few areas, especially in central Illinois, the two broods overlapped, and billions of red-eyed insects filled the trees with their deafening mating calls.
Periodical cicadas spend nearly their entire lives underground as nymphs, subsisting on sap from tree roots. (B) Then, when the soil reaches the right temperature in the right year, they emerge virtually simultaneously, ascend the nearest trunk, shed their skins, mate, lay eggs, and die within a few weeks. Because they appear in such overwhelming numbers, birds and other predators ____, and enough cicadas survive to produce the next generation.
Biologists have long been intrigued by the length of the cycles. (C) Both 13 and 17 are prime numbers. (D) Some researchers believe this is no accident: a predator with a shorter cycle of, say, two or three years would rarely reach its population peak in the same year as the cicadas. (E) Prime-numbered cycles may also diminish the chances that broods of different lengths emerge together and interbreed.

Approximately a thousand years ago, a woman who served the empress of Japan, remembered today as Sei Shonagon, filled a private notebook. Its contents were unlike anything else written in her time. Alongside anecdotes about court life and incisive portraits of her colleagues, she compiled lists under headings like Hateful Things, Things That Quicken the Pulse, and Things That Have Lost Their Power. A sparrow feeding its young, she wrote, quickens the pulse; so does washing one's hair and putting on fine clothes, even when no one will see.
The Pillow Book, as the work came to be called, was never meant to be a meticulously organized treatise. Its entries leap from one subject to another, and its judgments are often <u>caustic</u>: she mocks clumsy lovers, pretentious clerics, and guests who linger too long. Yet the very freedom of the form lets readers a thousand years later hear a distinct personal voice, witty, vain, and endlessly observant.
Scholars reckon the book among the founding works of a Japanese genre called zuihitsu, a name usually rendered as following the brush, whose authors let one thought lead freely to the next. Its enduring appeal suggests that a collection of fragments can encapsulate a life and an age as vividly as a single sustained narrative.

In the rainforests of Central and South America live small green frogs whose bellies are so transparent that an onlooker can see their hearts pulsating and their organs at work. These glass frogs spend their days asleep on the undersides of leaves, and their (A) ____ bodies let them merge almost perfectly with the light filtering through the foliage. Yet one part of the body had long perplexed biologists. Blood is red and should stand out clearly against a green leaf.
A study published in 2022 furnished an answer. Using a light-based imaging technique, researchers found that when a glass frog falls asleep, it sequesters nearly 90 percent of its red blood cells from circulation and stows them in its liver, which is covered by a reflective, mirror-like membrane. The frog's transparency roughly doubles or triples. Once the frog wakes up and starts moving, its blood cells flow back into circulation.
The finding is (B) ____ for a reason beyond camouflage. In most animals, people included, cramming blood cells together this tightly would cause dangerous clots. Glass frogs somehow evade this every night, and researchers hope that understanding how they accomplish it could eventually suggest new ways to prevent clotting in human patients.

When the 2025 World Expo opened in Osaka in April, its most conspicuous feature was not any single national pavilion but a structure that encompassed them all. The Grand Ring, designed by the architect Sou Fujimoto, is an elevated wooden walkway about two kilometers around, built predominantly of Japanese cedar and cypress and assembled with methods inspired by traditional joinery. Guinness World Records acknowledged it as the largest wooden architectural structure in the world.
World's fairs once acquainted the public with marvels such as the telephone, the ice cream cone, and the moving walkway. In an age when new technology arrives on every smartphone, critics have queried whether <u>such gatherings</u> still serve any purpose, and the Osaka Expo faced complaints about escalating construction costs and sluggish early ticket sales. Attendance nevertheless surged over the following months, and by the time the six-month event closed in October, more than twenty-five million visits had been tallied.
The fate of the ring itself became a subject of public controversy. Most of the structure was planned to be dismantled, but a section was earmarked for preservation, and some of the timber is anticipated to be reused. Supporters contend that the ring shows how expos can still ____, offering a communal physical experience that no screen can reproduce.

In the early 1990s, the Harvard physics professor Eric Mazur discovered that his students could solve complicated textbook problems yet floundered on simple questions about the concepts behind them. His lectures, which students lauded, had apparently taught them to utilize formulas without understanding why the formulas worked.
(A) During the discussion, something unforeseen happens. Students who have just grasped an idea are often more adept at explaining it than the professor, because they still remember what made it perplexing. When the class votes again, the share of correct answers typically surges.
(B) Mazur responded by changing how he taught. In his method, now known as peer instruction, the lecture is punctuated every few minutes by a conceptual question. Students first answer independently and then turn to their neighbors, trying to convince them that their answer is right.
(C) Studies at many universities have since found that classes taught this way produce more substantial gains in conceptual understanding than traditional lectures. The approach also redefines the role of the teacher, who becomes less a source of answers than a designer of incisive questions, one whose ____ is to provoke productive dissent.

Television comedies of the 1950s faced a predicament that live theater never had. On stage, an audience's laughter tells actors when to pause and tells spectators that a joke has landed. A program filmed in a studio without an audience, or transmitted into living rooms where viewers sat alone or in small groups, was deprived of this cue. One solution came from a sound engineer named Charles Douglass, who built a machine, often called the laff box, that could play recorded laughter of different lengths and intensities at the press of a key.
Producers soon added canned laughter to many sitcoms, and later research suggested why it worked: people are inclined to laugh more, and rate jokes as funnier, when they hear others laughing. Laughter, it seems, is less a private reaction to humor than a social signal, and hearing it ____.
Critics, however, complained that the technique was manipulative, dictating to viewers when to be amused rather than letting them decide for themselves. Since the early 2000s, many acclaimed comedies have jettisoned the laugh track altogether, relying on brisk editing and awkward silences instead. Some viewers who grew up with the older style now find shows without it eerily quiet, while many younger viewers find canned laughter distracting.

Rent control, which limits how much landlords may raise rents, is one of the most hotly debated policies in urban economics. Its allure is easy to comprehend. When housing costs escalate faster than wages, tenants who have lived in a neighborhood for decades may be evicted, and a cap on rent increases offers them (A) ____ against abrupt displacement.
Most economists, however, have long been skeptical. A widely cited study of San Francisco, published in 2019, found that a 1994 expansion of rent control did help covered tenants stay in their homes. Yet many landlords responded by converting their buildings to condominiums or other uses, curtailing the supply of rental housing in those buildings by about 15 percent. The curtailed supply, the authors contended, probably inflated rents elsewhere in the city, partly offsetting the policy's benefits.
Defenders of rent control reply that its purpose is not efficiency but stability for communities, and that the alternative, building far more housing, takes decades. Many cities now experiment with softer versions that allow moderate annual increases. The controversy suggests that rent control may be better at safeguarding current tenants than at (B) ____ the housing shortage itself.

The brushes hung in a neat row above the workbench, sorted by width, their handles dark with decades of paint. Mrs. Kang had lettered shop signs by hand in the old market district for forty years, and when her granddaughter Jiwon was sent to help her during the school holidays, the girl made no secret of deeming the work futile. Anyone could print a sign in an afternoon, she said. (A)
Mrs. Kang did not argue. She handed Jiwon a board and a pot of black enamel and asked her to paint a single letter, the R in RICE, over and over until the curve looked effortless. (B) By the end of the first week Jiwon's wrist throbbed, and her letters still wobbled.
In the second week a patron arrived: the owner of a noodle shop whose printed sign had faded to a wan gray after two summers in the sun. He wanted something durable. Mrs. Kang let Jiwon mix the colors and paint the shadow behind each letter while she did the main strokes herself. (C)
When the sign was hoisted, the old man stood across the street for a long time, beaming. Jiwon caught herself scrutinizing the curve of the R. (D) Then she retrieved a scrap board and, without being asked, began painting the letter anew. That evening she asked whether she could come back the next holiday, and Mrs. Kang, cleaning the brushes, simply nodded. (E)

City dwellers have long intuited that parks and tree-lined streets make them feel better, and a burgeoning body of research substantiates the intuition. One large Danish study, published in 2019, followed nearly a million people and found that those who grew up with more green space around their homes had a diminished risk of developing a range of psychiatric afflictions later in life. Other studies have linked even brief walks in a park to (A) ____ levels of stress hormones and improved mood. In one experiment in Philadelphia, researchers rehabilitated hundreds of vacant lots and planted them with grass and trees, and residents living nearby later reported feeling despondent considerably less often than those near lots that had been left alone.
Researchers caution that such findings do not demonstrate that greenery itself is responsible. Affluent neighborhoods tend to have more parks, and wealth also safeguards mental health in many ways. Still, the pattern has persisted in studies that try to account for income, and city planners have taken heed.
One widely cited guideline, proposed by the urban forester Cecil Konijnendijk, is known as the 3-30-300 rule: every resident should be able to see at least three trees from home, every neighborhood should have at least 30 percent tree canopy, and no one should live more than 300 meters from a park or green space. Several European cities have adopted variants of the rule as a planning goal, although the targets remain (B) ____ in densely built districts, where space for new trees is scarce and old pipes and cables clutter the ground beneath the pavement.

For most of the space age, only government astronauts, selected and groomed over many years, could leave the planet. That has begun to change. Since 2021, companies such as Blue Origin and Virgin Galactic have flown paying customers and invited guests on brief suborbital excursions, on which passengers ascend just above the conventional boundary of space and savor a few minutes of weightlessness before returning to Earth. In September 2024, the privately funded Polaris Dawn mission went further: two of its crew members emerged partly from their SpaceX capsule in the first spacewalk carried out by private citizens.
Supporters contend that such flights are the <u>vanguard</u> of a much broader enterprise. Revenue from affluent passengers, they say, helps subsidize reusable rockets and other technologies that could eventually lower the cost of reaching orbit for scientists, universities, and smaller countries.
Critics are less sanguine. Each launch burns copious amounts of fuel for the benefit of a handful of people, and some atmospheric scientists fret about soot released high in the atmosphere, where it lingers far longer than it does near the ground. Others dispute whether a ride lasting minutes should confer on its passengers the title of astronaut, and regulators continue to deliberate how much safety oversight a private passenger flight requires.

In late December 2024, a telescope in Chile detected a small asteroid, later named 2024 YR4, a few days after it had passed close to Earth. Estimated at roughly 40 to 90 meters across, it was far too small to imperil civilization but large enough to devastate a city if it struck a populous area. As astronomers tracked it, the calculated probability that it would hit Earth in December 2032 kept rising, briefly reaching about 3 percent in February 2025, the highest figure ever recorded for an object of its size.
The escalating numbers unnerved some members of the public, but astronomers were unperturbed. When an asteroid is first discovered, its orbit is known only approximately, and the range of possible paths is wide. If Earth happens to lie within that range, the probability of impact can rise as observations accumulate, even if the asteroid will eventually ____. That is precisely what transpired: further observations narrowed its probable trajectory, and within weeks the risk of hitting Earth had dropped to nearly zero.
The episode was nonetheless an instructive rehearsal for planetary defense. In 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft had deliberately collided with a small asteroid and measurably altered its orbit, showing that such a nudge is possible if a menace is detected early enough.

Virtually everyone knows the exasperating feeling of being certain that a word is lodged in memory yet being unable to retrieve it. In 1966, the Harvard psychologists Roger Brown and David McNeill set out to study this state in the laboratory. They read definitions of obscure words, such as a navigational instrument used to measure angles, and asked students to name the word being defined.
When students found the word on the tip of the tongue, Brown and McNeill asked them what they could recall. The results were striking. Even without retrieving the word, participants could often conjecture its first letter and its number of syllables, and they offered words with similar sounds, such as secant or sextet for the target word sextant. The word, it seemed, was not lost but partially ____: its contour was available even when its full form was not.
Later research has found that tip-of-the-tongue states become more frequent with age and with fatigue, and that they are usually resolved within a minute or so, often after the person stops trying. Bilingual speakers also report them somewhat more often, perhaps because they must juggle two vocabularies at once.

Imagine an eminent scientist named Mary who has spent her entire life in a black-and-white room. Through books and a black-and-white television, she has learned every physical fact there is to know about color: the wavelengths of light, the anatomy of the eye, the activity of the brain when someone looks at a ripe tomato. One day the door opens and Mary sees red for the first time. Does she learn something new?
The philosopher Frank Jackson, who devised this thought experiment in 1982, contended that she manifestly does: she learns what it is like to see red. If so, he inferred, knowing all the physical facts is not the same as knowing everything, and the purely physical picture of the mind must be (A) ____.
Critics have offered several rebuttals. Some argue that Mary acquires no new fact but only a new ability, such as the capacity to recognize or imagine red. Others posit that our intuition about her case is dubious, because no human could actually know all the physical facts. Remarkably, Jackson himself later recanted and came to defend physicalism, the very position his argument had been devised to assail. The puzzle nonetheless remains one of the most (B) ____ in the philosophy of mind, discussed in countless books and classrooms.

Do all languages divide the rainbow in the same way? For much of the twentieth century, many anthropologists presumed that color vocabulary was Ⓐ<u>arbitrary</u>, each culture slicing the spectrum wherever it pleased. In 1969, the anthropologist Brent Berlin and the linguist Paul Kay disputed that view. After comparing basic color terms in about one hundred languages, they reported a striking Ⓑ<u>regularity</u>.
Languages with only two basic color words, they found, differentiate dark from light. If a language has a third term, it is red. Next come green or yellow, then blue, then brown, and finally terms such as purple, pink, orange, and gray. A language with a word for blue almost always has words for red and green, but the reverse is often not true. The sequence appeared to be Ⓒ<u>haphazard</u>, as if languages climbed the same ladder one rung at a time.
Later research has Ⓓ<u>refined</u> the picture. Some languages do not conform to the sequence neatly, and the original study relied heavily on dictionaries and on speakers living far from their home communities. Even so, the broad pattern has largely endured, and most researchers now believe it reflects both the way the human eye responds to light and the Ⓔ<u>practical</u> needs of each culture. Color words, it seems, are shaped by ____ rather than by culture alone or biology alone.

For about two weeks each year, usually in late May or early June, visitors congregate at night in a forest in the Great Smoky Mountains of the United States to watch a remarkable spectacle. Thousands of fireflies of the species Photinus carolinus flash in unison, the whole hillside lighting up and going dark together in waves. So many people now come that the national park admits viewers through a lottery.
Only the males flash in these bursts. Each produces a brisk series of flashes followed by several seconds of darkness, and the females on the ground reciprocate with their own light. For decades scientists debated how thousands of insects could keep time without a leader. Studies suggest that each firefly modulates its rhythm slightly in response to the flashes of its neighbors, so that order emerges from countless local interactions rather than from any central signal.
Why synchronize at all? One hypothesis is that coordinated flashing makes the species' pattern easier for females to recognize amid the visual noise of other species and random flashes. Whatever its purpose, the display has become a quintessential example of how complex patterns in nature can arise ____.

In 1989, the British epidemiologist David Strachan noticed a peculiar pattern. Children who grew up with many older siblings were less susceptible to hay fever and eczema than children from smaller families. He postulated that early exposure to infections, transmitted among brothers and sisters, might help calibrate the developing immune system.
(A) These microbes, which live in soil, in animals, and on unprocessed food, have accompanied humans for most of our evolutionary history. Without habitual contact with them, the theory goes, the immune system may fail to learn restraint and <u>run amok</u>, assailing innocuous pollen, dust, or certain foods. For this reason, many researchers now prefer to speak of the old friends hypothesis, and they warn against abandoning basic hygiene, which still forestalls serious disease.
(B) The idea, which came to be called the hygiene hypothesis, was quickly popularized as a warning that modern homes had become too clean. That version, however, was misleading. Later research suggested that mundane household cleaning has little to do with the rise in allergies.
(C) What seems to matter instead is exposure to a particular set of microorganisms, which some scientists affectionately dub our old friends.

On the night of May 10, 2024, people across much of the Northern Hemisphere looked up to see something many had never witnessed: the sky glowing pink, green, and purple. (A) The aurora, usually confined to high latitudes such as northern Scandinavia, Canada, and Alaska, was photographed as far south as Mexico and northern India. (B) It was the upshot of the strongest geomagnetic storm to strike Earth in more than twenty years.
The storm began on the Sun. (C) A cluster of sunspots unleashed a series of coronal mass ejections, colossal clouds of charged particles that hurtled across space toward Earth's magnetic field. (D) The Sun was approaching the apex of its roughly eleven-year cycle of activity, when such eruptions are most frequent.
For most observers, the storm was a spectacle. For engineers, it was a sobering reminder of a hidden ____. Potent geomagnetic storms can induce electrical currents in long power lines, disrupt satellite navigation, and increase drag on satellites in low orbit. (E) In 1989, a storm precipitated a blackout across the Canadian province of Quebec that lasted about nine hours. The 2024 storm caused only negligible disruptions, partly because forecasters had warned power companies and satellite operators in advance.

In ancient Athens, many public offices were filled not by election but by lot, on the theory that any citizen was competent to serve and that random selection deterred the rich from buying power. The idea has enjoyed a modest resurgence. In 2016, Ireland convened a Citizens' Assembly of ninety-nine randomly chosen members of the public, selected to reflect the country's population in age, gender, and region, along with a chairperson.
Over several months of weekend meetings, the members heard testimony from experts, read submissions from the public, and deliberated in small groups. On the profoundly divisive question of abortion, they advocated changes that went further than many politicians had expected. When the question was put to voters in a 2018 referendum, the result broadly corresponded to the assembly's (A) ____ direction.
Supporters argue that such assemblies allow ordinary people to deliberate dispassionately on issues that elected politicians, apprehensive about losing votes, prefer to sidestep. Critics retort that members selected by lot are accountable to no one and that their recommendations carry (B) ____ democratic authority unless voters or parliaments approve them. Several countries, from France to Belgium, have since experimented with comparable bodies on topics ranging from climate policy to constitutional reform.

Today an address seems as natural as a name, yet for most of history dwellings in European cities had no numbers at all. A letter might be dispatched to a merchant opposite the church or at the sign of the golden lion, and visitors navigated by asking neighbors. Systematic numbering emerged not to help travelers but to serve the state.
In 1770, the Habsburg empress Maria Theresa decreed that every house in her lands be numbered so that officials could tally the men available for military service. Teams of clerks daubed numbers on doorways across whole provinces, often running consecutively through an entire town rather than street by street. Many residents resented the numbers, shrewdly suspecting that they would make it easier for the authorities to find, tax, and conscript them.
Other governments followed for comparable reasons. Paris adopted a new scheme in 1805, with even numbers on one side of the street and odd numbers on the other, a pattern later emulated around the world. Over time the numbers lost their association with soldiers and tax collectors and became a mundane convenience that delivery drivers and visitors rely on without a second thought. The history of the house number shows that tools introduced for ____ can end up serving everyday life.

Daniel carries a flashlight on his rounds, but he seldom needs to switch it on. At two in the morning the tanks of the city aquarium glimmer faintly blue, and the only sounds are the hum of the pumps and the muted tap of his shoes on the tiles. He took the night security job eight months ago, after the restaurant he had run for eleven years closed, and he still thinks of it as provisional. (A)
His favorite stop is the large tank where a venerable loggerhead turtle, known to the staff as Granny, drifts in languid circles. The keepers say she is more than sixty years old and was rescued from a fishing net long before any of them were hired. (B) Lately Daniel has begun confiding in her about his day, or rather his night: the broken lock on the loading door, the letter from the bank, the son who calls less often than he used to. (C)
Tonight he finds a drawing taped to the glass, left by a child during the afternoon. It shows a turtle with an enormous smile and, beside it, a stick figure clutching a flashlight. Underneath, in lopsided letters, someone has written: thank you for watching her at night.
Daniel stands there for a long time. (D) He has applied for three restaurant jobs this month and has been turned down by all of them. For the first time, though, he is not sure he would accept an offer if one came. (E)

When the record wildfires that swept through the mountains of southeastern Korea in March 2025 were finally put out, the first instinct of many residents and officials was to replant the blackened slopes as expeditiously as possible. Restoration ecologists advocate a more circumspect approach, one whose lessons apply far beyond Korea.
A burned forest is not necessarily a dead one. Many broadleaf trees, such as oaks, can resprout from their roots within a year or two, and seeds sequestered in the soil may germinate once sunlight reaches the ground. In such places, rushing in with heavy machinery and seedlings can do more harm than good, compacting the soil and trampling young growth. On the other hand, where fire has burned so hot that it obliterated the seeds in the soil, or where steep slopes risk landslides in the summer rains, active planting may be indispensable. Ecologists also point out that dead standing trees, though unsightly, shelter birds and insects and slowly return nutrients to the soil as they decay.
The choice of species also matters. Dense plantations of a single kind of conifer, favored after earlier fires because they grow quickly, tend to be highly flammable, and some researchers argue that they helped stoke the recent blazes. Mixing in fire-resistant broadleaf species could make the next forest less vulnerable. The lesson, ecologists say, is that restoration should ____: first scrutinize what the land is already doing, then intervene only where nature cannot regenerate on its own.

For several generations, a university degree has been touted to young people as the surest route into the middle class. In many countries, however, the price of that route has escalated far faster than wages. In the United States, outstanding federal student loans now exceed 1.6 trillion dollars, owed by more than 40 million borrowers, and some graduates are still repaying their loans well into middle age.
Governments have responded in markedly divergent ways. In 2023, the US Supreme Court invalidated a plan that would have canceled up to 20,000 dollars of debt for many borrowers, ruling that the administration had exceeded its authority. England levies some of the highest tuition fees in Europe but ties repayment to income, so graduates who earn little pay little, and remaining balances are written off after several decades. Germany, by contrast, had abolished tuition fees at its public universities by the middle of the 2010s.
Economists disagree about which model is fairest. Free tuition, its critics contend, largely <u>underwrites</u> the education of students from wealthier families, who are more apt to attend university in the first place. Defenders retort that high fees deter capable students from impoverished backgrounds, and that a well-educated population enriches everyone, not only the graduates themselves. Behind the dispute lies an older question: who should pay for higher education, the students who benefit directly or society as a whole?

More than 100,000 people in the United States are waiting for an organ transplant, most of them for a kidney, and thousands die each year before one becomes available. For decades, researchers have pursued an unorthodox solution: organs from pigs, whose kidneys are comparable in size to human ones. The impediment has always been rejection. The human immune system assails pig tissue within minutes, (A) ____ it as dangerously foreign.
Advances in gene editing have altered the picture. Companies now breed pigs with dozens of genetic modifications, excising pig genes that provoke the strongest immune reactions and adding human genes that help the organ coexist with its new body. In March 2024, surgeons at Massachusetts General Hospital transplanted such a kidney into a living patient for the first time. He died about two months later, though the hospital said there was no sign that the kidney had caused his death. Later recipients have lived with pig kidneys for several months, and regulators approved the first formal clinical trials in 2025.
The work raises misgivings as well as hopes. Some critics fret about the welfare of animals bred for their organs, and others about the risk of pig viruses crossing into humans. Supporters reply that the dearth of human organs is so (B) ____ that every promising avenue merits exploration.

In 1961, the psychologist Albert Bandura of Stanford University conducted a study that would become one of the most renowned in the field. Children aged approximately three to six were brought one at a time into a playroom. Some watched an adult quietly assemble toys; others watched an adult spend several minutes pummeling, kicking, and bellowing at an inflatable clown known as a Bobo doll.
Afterward, each child was taken to another room full of alluring toys, mildly exasperated by being told that the best ones were earmarked for other children, and then left alone with a Bobo doll. Children who had seen the aggressive adult were far more prone to attack the doll, often mimicking the adult's exact words and blows. Those who had watched the calm adult rarely did.
The study bolstered Bandura's argument that people learn not only from their own rewards and punishments but by watching others, a process he called observational learning. It challenged the view, then dominant, that behavior is shaped mainly through direct ____. Critics later disputed whether hitting a toy designed to be hit genuinely counts as aggression, but the broader notion that children copy the models around them has held up in many later studies.

In 1933, the German psychologist Hedwig von Restorff published a series of memory experiments with a deceptively simple design. Participants studied short lists of items for a few moments and then tried to recall as many of them as they could.
(A) Participants retained the odd item far better than the items around it. The finding, now known as the isolation effect or the von Restorff effect, has been corroborated many times since: an item that stands out from its surroundings is more likely to be noticed and later recalled, whether it differs in color, size, meaning, or sound.
(B) Advertisers and teachers have long exploited the effect, using bold colors, startling images, or unusual examples to make key points memorable. But the strategy has a limit. When too many items on a page are made to stand out, ____, and the advantage quietly evaporates.
(C) In most of the lists, virtually all the items belonged to one category, such as three-digit numbers. One item, however, was different in kind: a syllable or a small patch of color placed among the numbers, for example.

In December 1893, readers of The Strand Magazine opened the latest Sherlock Holmes story to find that the great detective had plunged to his death at the Reichenbach Falls in Switzerland, locked in a struggle with his archenemy, Professor Moriarty. The author, Arthur Conan Doyle, had grown weary of his creation. He deemed his historical novels far more serious work and lamented that Holmes kept him from loftier things.
The public reaction astonished him. Thousands of readers are said to have canceled their subscriptions to the magazine, and Doyle received irate letters from strangers, one of which reportedly began with the words You brute. For eight years, Doyle withstood <u>the pressure</u>. Then, in 1901, he began serializing The Hound of the Baskervilles, carefully set at a time before Holmes's fatal struggle. Two years later, in The Adventure of the Empty House, he resurrected the detective for good, explaining that Holmes had survived the fall and spent the intervening years roaming in disguise.
The episode is often cited as an early example of a modern phenomenon: the conviction among ardent fans that a beloved character belongs as much to them as to the author. Doyle had created Holmes, but by the 1890s he could no longer ____.

In 2021, Russian scientists reported that they had revived minuscule animals frozen in Siberian permafrost for about 24,000 years. The creatures were bdelloid rotifers, multicellular animals less than a millimeter long that live in fresh water and damp soil. After thawing, the rotifers not only began to move and feed but also reproduced, (A) ____ that they had survived the long freeze intact.
Bdelloid rotifers were already renowned among biologists for another reason. For tens of millions of years, as far as anyone can ascertain, they have reproduced without males. Their populations consist entirely of females that produce daughters from unfertilized eggs. Because sex shuffles genes and helps species adapt, most lineages that abandon it are thought to perish quickly, which makes the long survival of bdelloids a puzzle that one biologist called an evolutionary scandal.
Part of the answer may be that they borrow genetic material from other organisms. Studies have found that a surprisingly substantial share of their genes came from bacteria, fungi, and plants, perhaps assimilated when the animals dry out and later mend their damaged cells. Their extraordinary (B) ____ to freezing and drying may thus be linked to the unusual way they acquire new genes.

Passengers on Japanese trains occasionally notice something peculiar. Before the train departs, the driver points at a signal and calls out its status aloud, then points at the speedometer and calls out the speed, even when no one else is in the cab. Station staff do the same as they check the platform. To visitors the ritual can look theatrical, but it is a deliberate safety technique known as pointing and calling.
The method dates back more than a century to Japanese railway workers, and its rationale is simple. Routine tasks invite the mind to drift; an employee who has checked the same signal thousands of times may glance at it without truly seeing it. By forcing the eyes, hands, mouth, and ears to work together, pointing and calling turns each check into a conscious act. A study conducted in Japan in the 1990s reported that the practice reduced errors in a simple task by as much as 85 percent.
Despite such results, the technique has been slow to spread abroad. Workers elsewhere often find it embarrassing, and managers <u>balk at</u> rules that seem to treat skilled staff like children. A few railways outside Japan, including the New York City subway, have adopted variants of it, usually after a spate of accidents.

In 2025, a small furry monster with pointed ears and a mischievous grin full of jagged teeth became one of the most sought-after toys in the world. (A) Labubu, a character created by the Hong Kong-born artist Kasing Lung and sold by the Chinese company Pop Mart, drew throngs that lined up for hours outside stores from Bangkok to London. (B) Celebrities photographed with the dolls dangling from their handbags helped elevate a niche collectible into a global fashion accessory.
Much of the allure lies in the way the toys are sold. Most come in blind boxes, sealed packages whose contents remain concealed until they are opened. A buyer may covet a particular design but cannot know which one is inside, and rare editions appear in only a small fraction of boxes. (C)
Psychologists note that this arrangement resembles what researchers call a variable reward schedule, the same pattern that makes slot machines so hard to walk away from. (D) Because the reward arrives unpredictably, each purchase carries a small thrill of anticipation, and a disappointing box can feel less like a loss than like a reason to try again. (E) Some critics have warned that the format encourages ____ buying among young collectors, and resale prices for rare figures have at times skyrocketed to many times their original cost.

What do all games have in common? The question seems easy until one tries to answer it. In his Philosophical Investigations, published in 1953, two years after his death, Ludwig Wittgenstein invited readers to contemplate board games, card games, ball games, and the Olympic Games. Some involve winning and losing, but a child throwing a ball against a wall is not vying with anyone. Some require skill, others sheer luck. Some are played alone, others by teams.
Rather than a single feature shared by every game, Wittgenstein argued, we find an intricate network of similarities overlapping and crisscrossing, much as members of a family resemble one another in different ways: one shares a nose with her father, another the shape of her mother's eyes, yet no single trait runs through them all. He called this pattern family resemblance.
The idea challenged a venerable philosophical tradition, going back to Plato, which held that to comprehend a word we must pinpoint the essence that all its instances share. If Wittgenstein was right, many of our most useful concepts ____. This does not make them vague or useless; we apply the word game correctly every day without being able to define it.

In 1565, the Flemish painter Pieter Bruegel the Elder completed Hunters in the Snow, a wintry scene in which weary hunters and their dogs trudge home past a frozen pond teeming with skaters. Today the painting often appears on holiday cards, but some historians see in it a record of a harsher reality. Bruegel worked during the Little Ice Age, a period spanning roughly from the fourteenth to the nineteenth century in which European winters were, on average, perceptibly colder than before. In 1709, a winter so severe that it became known as the Great Frost killed livestock and froze rivers across much of the continent.
The cooling was modest by modern standards, a matter of a degree or less in average temperature, yet its effects were (A) ____. Truncated growing seasons led to failed harvests and famine in several decades, and glaciers in the Alps encroached on farms and villages. In London, the River Thames froze solid often enough that residents held frost fairs on the ice, with booths, games, and even printing presses.
Scholars still dispute the causes, which may include a series of major volcanic eruptions and a period of anomalously low solar activity. Artists of the time, of course, were not trying to chronicle the climate. Still, art historians have discerned that winter landscapes became a (B) ____ subject in Dutch and Flemish painting during the coldest decades, suggesting that painters were responding, perhaps unconsciously, to the world outside their windows.

"Look where you want to go, not at what you're afraid of hitting," my father said. "The car follows your eyes."
We were in the empty parking lot behind the wholesale market on a Sunday morning, and I was clutching the wheel so hard that my knuckles had turned white. (A) The only obstacle in the whole lot was a single concrete post near the exit, and I had already managed to drive toward it twice, staring at it in dread as the car crept closer.
My father did not grab the wheel or raise his voice. He simply asked me to stop, breathe, and pick a point beyond the post: a blue gate at the far end of the lot. (B) On the next try, I glanced back at the post at the last moment and swerved away only at the last second. On the one after that, I scraped past it with a hand's width to spare, my eyes locked on the concrete. (C)
Then I kept my eyes on the blue gate and felt the car curve gently, virtually by itself, around the obstacle. (D) When I stopped, my father was chuckling quietly, the first sound he had made in several minutes. Neither of us alluded to the post, and he let me drive us all the way home.
I passed my driving test that winter. But the lesson I still use has little to do with cars. <u>Whatever we stare at in fear, we tend to steer toward.</u> (E)
